sn56.11:1.1: This is the Buddha’s first discourse proper. In the narrative following the Buddha’s awakening ([pli-tv-kd1:6.16.9]()), it follows the apparently fruitless encounter with Upaka on the road from Bodhgaya to Varanasi ([mn26:25.1](), and precedes the teaching on not-self ([sn22.59]()). It is included in full in the later treatise the Paṭisambhidāmagga ([ps2.6:1.1]()), and is alluded to many times in the Suttas, sometimes by name ([mn141:32.1]()), sometimes implicitly ([mn26:29.1]()). It is still a key text in Theravāda Buddhism, and is regularly memorized and recited. The Saṅgha at the Deer Park recite it every night.
sn56.11:1.2: These are the ascetics with whom the Bodhisatta practiced before rejecting their path of extreme asceticism ([mn36:20.2]()). The Buddha has traveled especially to teach them out of gratitude, because they were very helpful to him ([mn26:24.5]()). Their names are listed in the Vinaya account: Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, and Assaji ([pli-tv-kd1:6.31.6]()). | Note that he calls them “mendicants”, a term typically reserved for Buddhist renunciates. For a similar usage, see [mn140:3.4](). In the Vinaya account, they ordained after this teaching.
sn56.11:2.3: The Buddha begins by finding common ground with the ascetics—the rejection of sensual pleasures, repudiating their idea that he had given himself up to luxury (see [dn29:23.2.]()). Only then does he reject the five ascetics’ own practice of self-mortification. The descriptions in the Suttas make it clear that these practices were closely allied to the Jains, although the Buddha does not formally identify them ([mn85:10.2]())
sn56.11:9.1: The related passage at AN 8.64 suggests that the tiparivaṭṭaṁ dvādasākāraṁ apply to the knowledge, not the truths.
